title: From Fast and Furious to Walking Fentanyl: Lessons Not Learned by the US
author: Nancy Flores
content:
_This article by[Nancy
Flores](https://contralinea.com.mx/author/nancy_contra/) originally appeared
in the [September 19, 2026 edition of
Contralínea](https://contralinea.com.mx/investigacion/del-rapido-y-furioso-al-
walking-fentanyl-lecciones-no-aprendidas-por-eu/), a Mexican investigative
journalism magazine._

_Documents and emails declassified by the US government on the failed Fast and
Furious operation —agreed upon by the administrations of Felipe Calderón and
Barack Obama— reveal similarities with the Walking Fentanyl operation.
Although the agencies in charge are different —in the first case it was the
ATF and, in the second, the DEA—, both were carried out knowing they would
cause deaths; in both, the violation of US laws was authorized in order,
supposedly, to learn the inner workings of the crimes, and the US border was
opened to give free passage both to the trafficking of weapons and to that of
fentanyl. Another feature they share is that they failed: the agencies did not
land any decisive blow against the criminal networks that operate on US
territory. In the case of Fast and Furious, it also involved the intentional
violation of Mexican laws; in addition, it contributed to the increase in
deadly violence in the north of the country: the weapons were handed over to
the Sinaloa Cartel, an organization to which the then-federal Secretary of
Public Security and Calderón 's right-hand man was allied._

**Second and final part.** As the United States was ramping up its intrusion
into Mexico through the Mérida Initiative —one of the main sources of funding
for the supposed "war" on drug trafficking waged by Felipe Calderón and his
secretary Genaro García Luna—, between 2009 and 2010 the operation Fast and
Furious (Rápido y Furioso) was carried out, allowing some **2,000 high-caliber
weapons** to be trafficked to the Sinaloa Cartel.

Led by Group VII of the Phoenix Division —of the ATF (Bureau of Alcohol,
Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives)— that failed "experiment" to learn about the
networks that made possible the illegal trafficking of weapons from the United
States to Mexico shares several similarities with the recently uncovered
operation Walking Fentanyl, carried out by the Drug Enforcement Administration
(DEA) during the past administration of Joe Biden.

Documents and emails declassified by the US government regarding the Fast and
Furious operation, as well as the announcement of the opening of an
investigation into the Walking Fentanyl operation, reveal that both were
carried out knowing they would cause deaths; in both, the violation of US laws
was authorized in order, supposedly, to learn the inner workings of the
crimes, and the border of the neighboring country to the north was opened to
give free passage to the trafficking of weapons and of fentanyl, respectively.

![Declassified US government documents on the Fast and Furious and Walking
Fentanyl operations](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/02-declassified-docs.png)Declassified US government
documents on the Fast and Furious and Walking Fentanyl operations.

Another feature of the two operations is their failure: neither the ATF nor
the DEA obtained information to dismantle the criminal networks that operate
in US territory and, with it, halt the illegal trafficking; nor did they land
any decisive blows against criminals on the other side of the border.

Additionally, in the case of Fast and Furious —an operation authorized by
Calderón's government— it involved the intentional violation of Mexican laws,
in addition to contributing to the increase in deadly violence in the north of
the country: the weapons were handed over to the Sinaloa Cartel, and members
of that organization —then associated with García Luna— removed the tracking
chips and used them to expand their firepower.

Faced with the US government's attempts to pressure Mexico on the false
argument that not enough is being done against drug trafficking, and its
threats to intervene in our country, this past September 10 President Claudia
Sheinbaum Pardo recalled these two cases as part of the problems that the
United States has not resolved in its own territory. She also observed that it
is part of the electoral fervor, and thus demanded that Mexico not be used to
try to win votes.

> It's, if you will, a 'Fast and Furious,' but over there; but with drugs, not
> weapons. So they have plenty of problems over there, or their own problems,
> without their campaigns devoting themselves to the issue of the United
> States. They have no reason to use Mexico in their electoral campaign.
>
> President Claudia Sheinbaum

She also exposed the contradictions US authorities constantly fall into: "some
days they say: 'no, Mexico is doing its job very well and we are coordinating
very well.' And another day: 'no, but they're not doing enough. Of course, if
Mexico does its job, then great; but, if not, well, there can be
consequences.' So, it's part of the campaign, from our point of view. And what
do we say? Let's coordinate, as we have done up to now, and each side runs its
campaigns on its own territory."

At that morning press conference, Sheinbaum Pardo recalled that the midterm
elections in the United States will be held this coming November, and thus
reiterated: "let them not use Mexico in their campaign. The United States has
its problems. So Mexico should not be used as part of the electoral campaign
of the United States."

## Investigation Against the DEA

Beyond the electoral campaign that the Trump administration is facing with low
popularity, the Walking Fentanyl operation would show that US agencies did not
learn the lesson that the Fast and Furious operation left the ATF.

This past August 31, Congressman James Comer sent a communication to Attorney
General Blanche, informing him that the Committee on Oversight and Government
Reform had opened an investigation into the "loosening," by the Joe Biden
administration, "of risk-mitigation protocols related to fentanyl." The letter
details that, through said operation, law enforcement was allegedly prevented
from intervening to stop the trafficking of the opioid.

"They allowed deadly street drugs to reach US communities. The first Trump
administration developed risk-mitigation protocols that addressed the unique
threat that fentanyl poses to public safety, requiring agents to make
reasonable efforts to prevent the distribution of this lethal drug. But the
Biden administration dismissed those protocols and, instead, allowed the
shipments to remain in the custody and control of criminals."

The document notes that, in early 2023, the DEA intentionally stopped applying
anti-drug-trafficking protocols in New Mexico: "instead, the DEA allowed
shipments of up to **100,000 pills** to remain in the hands of criminals,
giving rise to the practice of 'Walking Fentanyl,' in which the pills were not
intercepted and were allowed to keep moving through criminal networks. DEA
agents monitored the shipments of pills but did not seize them, allowing
hundreds of thousands of pills to reach the streets of New Mexico" between
January 21, 2021 and January 19, 2025.

In his letter, the congressman adds that, according to Biden government
officials, the objective of said operation was to build a larger case in order
to prosecute more criminals; however, the result was an increase in threats to
public safety. He adds that New Mexico was severely affected by fentanyl
trafficking, which is proven by the fact that a **nearly 21 percent increase
in deaths from poisoning by this substance was recorded, against a 14 percent
decrease in the rest of the country**.

![Excerpt from Congressman James Comer's letter on the Walking Fentanyl
operation](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/03-comer-
letter.png)Excerpt from Congressman James Comer's letter on the Walking
Fentanyl operation.

Regarding the protocols the DEA stopped applying, he explains that no
operations were carried out to prevent the drug from reaching the streets of
New Mexico, no search warrants were requested, and the fentanyl was not
seized; instead, it was allowed to "walk."

And although he acknowledged the likelihood that DEA agents do not have
sufficient resources to intercept all the shipments they are aware of, he
pointed out that "a policy ordering them not to intercept significant
shipments is unacceptable and, without a doubt, caused considerable harm and
the loss of lives." According to the DEA, due to the devastating effects of
fentanyl, **more than 50,000 people died in 2024; and nearly 80,000, in
2023**.

In addition to Congressman Comer's notes, it stands out that the DEA kept the
Walking Fentanyl operation hidden, and that this became known only when the US
press revealed it. It also runs counter to other public policies of the Agency
itself, such as the "Fentanyl-Free United States" initiative. That one not
only focuses on controlling the opioid to reduce its supply, but also includes
awareness campaigns to curb demand.

The Agency details that the Sinaloa Cartel and the Jalisco New Generation
Cartel have modified their commercial practices: "DEA laboratory tests
indicate that 29 percent of the fentanyl pills analyzed during 2025 contained
a potentially lethal dose, a significant decrease from the 76 percent of pills
analyzed just two years earlier, in 2023. In addition, the purity of powdered
fentanyl decreased to 10.3 percent, compared to the 19.5 percent recorded
during the same period. The reduction in both potency and purity correlates
with a decline in deaths from synthetic opioids to levels not seen since April
2020."

## Lessons From Fast and Furious

The "Walking Fentanyl" operation reveals that US agencies did not learn the
lesson of the disastrous Fast and Furious operation, led by Group VII of the
Phoenix Division. In that case, the ATF let some 2,000 high-powered weapons
"walk" into Mexico, with the supposed objective of tracking them and
determining how the illegal trafficking of weaponry for the drug cartels
operated.

Declassified reports and emails from that operation detail the ATF's conduct:
in real time, the agency knew that the weapons trafficked with its consent
were increasing violence in Mexico and causing more and more murders.

An example of this are the emails that David J. Voth, supervisor of Phoenix
Group VII, sent to the other agents involved in the operation. On March 12,
2010, with the subject line: "Monday morning meeting, Strike Force, 9:30
a.m.," he told them: "I have been informed that a rift may be brewing within
the group. This is the moment when we should all come together, not split
apart. We all have a right to our respective opinions (even if they are
different); however, we must get along and understand that we have a mission
to accomplish.

"I am thrilled and proud that our group is the first of the ATF groups for the
country's southwest border to… [CENSORED]. That said, I thank you all for your
efforts to date and I applaud the results we have achieved in a short time.
Whether it matters to you or not, top brass and headquarters authorities are
following this case very closely and also believe that we (Phoenix Group VII)
are doing what the southwest border groups were conceived for. It may sound
corny, but we are 'the tip of the ATF's spear' when it comes to firearms
trafficking on the southwest border.

"We must resolve our problems at this meeting. I will not under any
circumstances allow this case to be harmed by trivial arguments, rumors, or
other adolescent-type behavior. I don't know what all the problems are, but we
are all adults, we are all professionals, and we have an exciting opportunity
to use the most important tool in our law enforcement arsenal. If you don't
think this is fun, you're in the wrong profession; and that's that! This is
the pinnacle of national US law enforcement techniques. After this, the
arsenal is empty. Maybe the Maricopa County jail is hiring detention officers
and you can earn 30,000 dollars (instead of 100,000) for serving lunch to
inmates all day.

"Finally, many of our fellow ATF agents are coming to town to help us on this
case. We must give our best and lead by example. No one wants to leave their
family behind or abandon their pending cases to help someone who doesn't even
value their sacrifice. We must overcome this obstacle once and for all and
move forward with the mission at hand. This may be the most fun experience
you'll have at the ATF; the only one who limits the fun is ourselves!"

![Declassified email from ATF supervisor David J. Voth to Group VII
agents](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/04-voth-email-
first.png)Declassified email from ATF supervisor David J. Voth to Group VII
agents.

Almost a month later, on March 2, 2010, David J. Voth again wrote to the
entire group and copied the then-prosecutor in Phoenix, Emory Hurley —also
involved in the Fast and Furious operation and who, after the scandal, was
reassigned from criminal to civil cases—, and George T. Gillett Jr., special
agent in charge of the ATF in Phoenix. The subject of the email was: "No
pressure, but perhaps with a greater sense of urgency…"

Its content was very telling, since it begins with a list illustrating the
violence in Mexico:

  * "958 dead in March 2010 (the most violent month since 2005)
  * "937 dead in January 2010
  * "842 dead in December 2009
  * "187 murders in March, including 11 police officers"

"I hope this email is well received, since it is not intended to imply
anything other than the fact that the violence in Mexico is serious and,
without meaning to be dramatic, we feel a sense of urgency regarding this
investigation. Our subjects bought 359 firearms in the month of March alone,
including numerous Barrett .50 caliber rifles. I believe our plan to dismantle
this entire organization is justified, and that rushing to arrest a single
person without taking into account the full scope of the conspiracy would be
inadvisable for the overall success of the mission. I recognize that we all
agree that doing it correctly requires patience and planning. Nonetheless, if
there were something we could do to facilitate a timely response or action by
others, we should communicate our sense of urgency regarding this matter.

"Thank you all for your continued support in this endeavor,

"David Voth

"Supervisor, Phoenix Group VII"

![Declassified email signed by David Voth, supervisor of Phoenix Group
VII](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/05-voth-
signature.png)Declassified email signed by David Voth, supervisor of Phoenix
Group VII.

A month later, on May 3, 2010, Voth himself wrote as the subject of the email:
"Just for your information…" And in the content, he pointed out to them:
"April was the second most violent month during the Calderón administration,
with 1,231 killings. This figure is more than double that recorded in the same
month of 2009 (560 deaths) and five times that of 2008 (270)."

![Declassified May 2010 email from David Voth on violence in
Mexico](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/06-voth-may-
email.png)Declassified email: "April was the second most violent month during
the Calderón administration."

Another document declassified by the US authorities, and identified as
"Phoenix Group VII (Firearms Trafficking GRIT/SWB) 785115-10-0004, Operation
Fast and Furious (Rápido y Furioso)," notes that said operation was part of "a
large-scale firearms trafficking investigation, in which weapons have been
recovered either in the Republic of Mexico or on the border between the United
States and Mexico (or in its immediate vicinity: El Paso, TX; Nogales, AZ;
Douglas, AZ, etc.). To date, more than 1,500 firearms have been acquired since
October 2009 —paying more than 1 million dollars in cash, through direct
transactions at various federally licensed establishments (FFL) in the Phoenix
area—. Currently, the ATF maintains active several judicially authorized audio
interceptions (under Title III regulations), and there are sworn statements
pending approval at the Department of Justice (Office of Enforcement
Operations, or DOJ-OEO) relating to other target phones linked to this
conspiracy. This investigation presents multiple strands: the ATF seeks not
only to prosecute various individuals for straw-purchase offenses or
unlicensed weapons dealing, but, more specifically, to establish the link with
the Mexican cartel or drug trafficking organization (DTO) that obtains said
weapons, in order to consolidate the strongest possible case and to bring the
most serious charges when the moment of formal accusation arrives."

![Declassified document on Operation Fast and Furious, Phoenix Group
VII](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/07-fast-furious-
document.png)Declassified document on Operation Fast and Furious (Phoenix
Group VII).

And another of the documents details how the weapons were being acquired and
how they were handed over to the traffickers: "on May 8, 2010, a cooperating
defendant of Task Force VIII of Group VII, of the ATF in Phoenix, participated
in the simulated purchase of firearms to later sell them to a trafficker." To
do so, the declassified report notes, he was asked to visit Lone Wolf Trading
Company and Arizona Auto Weapons, both holders of federal weapons-sale
licenses. There he was to acquire five Beretta 92SF pistols (9 mm,
semiautomatic). At the first business they had only two available, while at
the second, more than 40. He acquired two weapons, respectively (serial
numbers: 1159712 and J395712), and filled out ATF forms 4473 and 3310.4 during
the process.

"After returning to the area near the agent's residence, he met with ATF
Phoenix Task Force VIII at a previously agreed-upon neutral location. He
photographed the pistols, noted their serial numbers, and provided the
cooperator with an electronic audio-recording device. Subsequently, the agent
returned to the residence and informed him by telephone of his return. He
positioned himself in a nearby location suitable for surveillance.

"At approximately 5:00 p.m. on this date, a black Mitsubishi Eclipse
convertible was observed arriving at the cooperator's residence. Approximately
30 minutes later, the same black Mitsubishi convertible was observed leaving
the area. Shortly afterward, the cooperator was debriefed on the encounter
with an audio-recording device. During the debriefing, the cooperator
indicated that a person, driving the black Mitsubishi Eclipse convertible,
arrived at the residence; they spoke generally about possession of the two
Beretta 92SF pistols that the cooperator had purchased at LWTC. The person
paid him 200 dollars for the weapons. As evidenced in the audio recording
(which is part of this file and is incorporated into it), he informed the
agent that he would obtain little more profit than this from this (and other)
firearms transactions. He went on to describe how his financial needs were the
factor motivating him to traffic weapons and how he would continue doing so
until those needs were satisfied. In addition, he tried to reassure the agent
by stating that he assumed the only real risk in their trafficking arrangement
when he erased the serial numbers from the weapons and transported them south,
toward their final destination."

In the end, and as is already known, the Fast and Furious operation not only
failed, but it was found to have been responsible for supplying weaponry to
the Sinaloa Cartel and, consequently, also contributed to the violence and the
increase in intentional homicides in Mexico. It was even documented that some
of those weapons were used in the murders of US citizens. Following these
events, Group VII was dissolved. However, the case remains unpunished; so much
so that Felipe Calderón was never called to clarify his government's
participation in it.
